title: Three daily checks
hook: Zengzi examines himself three times daily: was I loyal, trustworthy, did I practice what I was taught? (Analects 1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tai chi: a fighting art softened into moving stillness, where the one who yields stays standing. Your line was moving stillness. When someone pushed, did you manage to give way a little first? Day one thousand four hundred six.

If you could check only three things about your day before you slept, which three would you choose? Not your steps or your screen time. Not your inbox. Three questions about who you were today. It's harder than it sounds. A list of ten is easy. Ten lets you hide. Three makes you decide what actually matters. A student of Confucius named Zengzi made that choice, and his answer is written into the opening pages of the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. It's short enough to fit on a sticky note. It still works as a nightly check. Yesterday we moved; today we stop and look back.
screen: `ONLY THREE THINGS. WHICH THREE?` → `TEN LETS YOU HIDE.` → `ZENGZI'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here is Zengzi, in James Legge's translation: "I daily examine myself on three points." And here are the three, in plain words. First: in working for someone else, was I faithful? Did I give their task my real effort, as if it were my own? Second: with my friends, was I true to my word? Did I say what I meant and do what I said? Third: what my teacher passed on to me, did I actually practice it? Look at what's not on the list. Nothing about success. Nothing about how others treated me. Nothing about feelings, or luck. All three are about the gap between what I owe and what I did. The check starts with the self, at close range, with the people right in front of you. And notice the word daily. Not once a year at a big turning point. Every day, small and plain, like brushing your teeth. There's a lovely puzzle in the third question, too. The Chinese is so compact it can be read two ways. Some readers take it as: did I practice what was passed on to me? Others take it as: did I pass on to others anything I hadn't practiced myself? One is about the student, the other about the teacher, and one person can be both. Either way, the check is the same: do my words and my life match? The questions don't ask for guilt. They ask for honesty, then for tomorrow. Zengzi doesn't say what he does with the answers. Maybe that's the point. The checking itself is the practice.
screen: `WAS I FAITHFUL IN WORK FOR OTHERS?` · `WAS I TRUE TO MY FRIENDS?` · `DID I PRACTICE WHAT I WAS TAUGHT?` · `READ TWO WAYS: STUDENT OR TEACHER.` · then, large: `I DAILY EXAMINE MYSELF ON THREE POINTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask the three. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think back over yesterday, or today so far. First question: when I did something for someone else, did I give it real effort? Let one moment come up, without judging it. Breathe. Second: with a friend, was I true to my word? Let one moment come. Breathe. Third: something I've learned, maybe on this path, did I live it, even once? Just notice the answers. No scolding. If you pray, you can bring what you found into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Three daily checks. Zengzi's daily questions in the Analects: was I faithful, was I true to my word, did I practice what I was taught. Today's word.

Your line: three checks. Tonight, before you sleep, ask Zengzi's three questions once more, about this whole day. Write the answers down if it helps. Keep it short and honest. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: People drawn to Confucian practice use Zengzi's three questions as a daily self-examination, often at the end of the day, sometimes keeping a journal of the answers.

original.note: Chinese, from Analects 1.4: three examinations of oneself.

trapdoor: what you thought: three daily checks sounds like a productivity habit.
what it means: Zengzi's daily questions about faithfulness, keeping his word, and living what he learned.
what a scholar hears: the third line is compact enough to read as either receiving or passing on teaching unpracticed.

sources.quoted: I daily examine myself on three points.

notes: Analects 1.4 opening is quoted from Legge 1861 from memory ('I daily examine myself on three points'); verify. The three points themselves are paraphrased, not quoted.
The double reading of 傳不習乎 (did I practice what was transmitted to me / did I transmit what I had not practiced) is stated as 'some readers / others'. Confirm both readings are fairly represented.
'Zengzi doesn't say what he does with the answers' refers to 1.4 alone. Confirm.

Editor pass: 'evening' and 'nightly' (word segment, trapdoor) became 'daily', since 1.4 names no time of day; 'Zengzi was both' (student and teacher, not in 1.4) became 'one person can be both'; 'that's very Confucian' became 'the check starts with the self'. Legge's opening line checked.
